sources.title: VAT registration timing — rolling 12 months and 30-day forward look
sources.excerpt: Rolling 12-month (backward) test: if at the end of any month your taxable supplies in the previous 12 months (or less) exceed £90,000, you must notify HMRC within 30 days of that month-end. Effective date of registration is typically the first day of the second month after you went over the threshold. Forward-looking 30-day test: if at any time you expect taxable supplies in the next 30 days alone to exceed £90,000, you must register by the end of that 30-day period; the effective date is the date you first formed that expectation. These are separate tests — do not confuse an 11-month build-up plus next month with the forward look. Always confirm on GOV.UK / VAT Notice 700/1.

results.question: Do I need to register for VAT at £85,000 turnover?
results.expected_tax_notes: Check current VAT threshold on GOV.UK (historically £90k) — verify page.
results.reply_unedited:
You must register for VAT if your total taxable turnover exceeds £90,000 in the last 12 months or if you expect it to exceed £90,000 in the next 30 days. The previous threshold of £90,000 is outdated. If your turnover is below £90,000, you do not need to register, but you can choose to do so voluntarily. For the most accurate and up-to-date information, please check GOV.UK. 

Do you need help with anything else regarding VAT registration?

sources.title: VAT registration threshold
sources.excerpt: You must register for VAT if either (1) your total taxable turnover for the last 12 months goes over £90,000 (the rolling / backward look, checked at month-end), or (2) you expect your taxable turnover to go over £90,000 in the next 30 days alone (the forward look). You can also register voluntarily below £90,000. The former £85,000 threshold is outdated and must not be used. Confirm current figures on GOV.UK.

sources.title: VAT registration timing — rolling 12 months and 30-day forward look
sources.excerpt: Rolling 12-month (backward) test: if at the end of any month your taxable supplies in the previous 12 months (or less) exceed £90,000, you must notify HMRC within 30 days of that month-end. Effective date of registration is typically the first day of the second month after you went over the threshold. Forward-looking 30-day test: if at any time you expect taxable supplies in the next 30 days alone to exceed £90,000, you must register by the end of that 30-day period; the effective date is the date you first formed that expectation. These are separate tests — do not confuse an 11-month build-up plus next month with the forward look. Always confirm on GOV.UK / VAT Notice 700/1.

sources.title: VAT registration timing — rolling 12 months and 30-day forward look
sources.excerpt: Rolling 12-month (backward) test: if at the end of any month your taxable supplies in the previous 12 months (or less) exceed £90,000, you must notify HMRC within 30 days of that month-end. Effective date of registration is typically the first day of the second month after you went over the threshold. Forward-looking 30-day test: if at any time you expect taxable supplies in the next 30 days alone to exceed £90,000, you must register by the end of that 30-day period; the effective date is the date you first formed that expectation. These are separate tests — do not confuse an 11-month build-up plus next month with the forward look. Always confirm on GOV.UK / VAT Notice 700/1.

sources.excerpt: You must register for VAT if either (1) your total taxable turnover for the last 12 months goes over £90,000 (the rolling / backward look, checked at month-end), or (2) you expect your taxable turnover to go over £90,000 in the next 30 days alone (the forward look). You can also register voluntarily below £90,000. The former £85,000 threshold is outdated and must not be used. Confirm current figures on GOV.UK.

sources.title: VAT registration timing — rolling 12 months and 30-day forward look
sources.excerpt: Rolling 12-month (backward) test: if at the end of any month your taxable supplies in the previous 12 months (or less) exceed £90,000, you must notify HMRC within 30 days of that month-end. Effective date of registration is typically the first day of the second month after you went over the threshold. Forward-looking 30-day test: if at any time you expect taxable supplies in the next 30 days alone to exceed £90,000, you must register by the end of that 30-day period; the effective date is the date you first formed that expectation. These are separate tests — do not confuse an 11-month build-up plus next month with the forward look. Always confirm on GOV.UK / VAT Notice 700/1.

results.reply_unedited:

1. **Check the Penalty Notice**: Review the notice to understand why the penalty was issued and the specific details.

2. **Gather Evidence**: Collect any relevant documents or information that support your case for appealing the penalty.

3. **Submit Your Appeal**: You can appeal online through your HMRC account or by writing to HMRC. Include your details, the penalty reference, and your reasons for the appeal.

4. **Wait for a Response**: HMRC will review your appeal and inform you of their decision.

Make sure to appeal within the specified time frame mentioned in the penalty notice. For more detailed guidance, refer to the official HMRC website. Would you like to know more about the types of penalties?

results.question: I transferred a property to my spouse. CGT?
results.expected_tax_notes: CGT/spouse rules — advice.
results.reply_unedited:
When you transfer a property to your spouse, it is generally treated as a "no gain, no loss" transaction for Capital Gains Tax (CGT) purposes. This means that you won't have to pay CGT at the time of the transfer, and your spouse will inherit your original cost basis in the property.

However, if your spouse later sells the property, they may be liable for CGT based on the increase in value from the time you originally acquired it. It's essential to keep detailed records of the property's value and any associated costs.

turns.user: I haven’t done my tax for two years. What happens?
turns.reply:
If you haven't submitted your Self Assessment tax returns for two years, you may face penalties and interest on any unpaid tax. HMRC can charge late filing penalties, which increase the longer you delay. Additionally, you could be subject to a tax investigation. It's important to address this as soon as possible to minimise penalties.

I recommend contacting HMRC to discuss your situation and consider seeking professional advice to help you get back on track. Would you like more information on how to proceed?

turns.user: Can you explain what I should do next?
turns.reply:
To address your overdue tax returns, follow these steps:

1. **Gather Records**: Collect all relevant income and expense records for the two years you missed. This includes bank statements, invoices, and receipts.

2. **Contact HMRC**: Reach out to HMRC to inform them of your situation. They can provide guidance on how to proceed and any penalties you may face.

3. **Complete Your Returns**: Prepare and submit your outstanding Self Assessment tax returns for both years. You can do this online through the HMRC portal or with the help of an accountant.

4. **Pay Any Tax Owed**: Once your returns are submitted, pay any tax due to avoid further penalties and interest.

5. **Consider Professional Help**: If you're unsure about the process, you might want to consult a tax professional for assistance.

turns.user: HMRC charged me a late filing penalty. Is that fair?
turns.reply:
HMRC imposes late filing penalties for Self Assessment tax returns if you miss the deadlines. The penalties are designed to encourage timely submissions. If you filed after the deadline, it is generally considered fair for HMRC to charge a penalty. The amount depends on how late the return is filed. 

If you believe there are extenuating circumstances or if you have a reasonable excuse, you can appeal the penalty. For detailed information on penalties, you can check the HMRC guidance on GOV.UK. Would you like to know more about the appeal process?

turns.user: Can you explain what I should do next?
turns.reply:
If you've received a late filing penalty from HMRC, here are the steps you can take:

1. **Review the Penalty Notice**: Check the details on the notice to understand the reason and amount of the penalty.

2. **Consider Your Circumstances**: If you have a reasonable excuse for the late filing (e.g., illness, natural disaster), gather any supporting evidence.

3. **Appeal the Penalty**: You can appeal online through your HMRC account or by writing to them. Include your reasons and any evidence.

4. **Pay the Penalty**: If you decide not to appeal or if your appeal is unsuccessful, ensure you pay the penalty to avoid further charges.

5. **Prevent Future Issues**: Consider setting reminders for future deadlines or seeking assistance with your Self Assessment to avoid late submissions.

If you need help with your Self Assessment or appealing the penalty, I can provide more information on our services. Would you like to explore that?

turns.user: Do I need to register for VAT at £85,000 turnover?
turns.reply:
You must register for VAT if your total taxable turnover exceeds £90,000 in the last 12 months or if you expect it to exceed £90,000 in the next 30 days. The previous threshold of £90,000 is outdated. If your turnover is below £90,000, you do not need to register, but you can choose to do so voluntarily. For the most accurate and up-to-date information, please check GOV.UK.
